newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia's ruling party on track for bigger vote.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia's ruling party on track for bigger vote.

text.p: Indonesia's ruling Golkar party said on Thursday it was on course to improve its share of the vote in next year's general elections to a targeted 71 percent from the 68 percent recorded in the previous polls.
"Golkar has (been promised) 70.25 percent of the vote according to reports that have been sent in by the regional branches up to October," party secretary-general Ary Mardjono told a news conference.
"It can still go up and down," Mardjono added.
Golkar chairman Harmoko (Eds: one word) said on Wednesday the ruling party hoped to improve its share of the vote at the poll.

"We have to increase our victory from what we gained in 1992. If Golkar got 68 percent then we would consider our victory solid if we could increase our number of votes in 1997," Harmoko, who is also minister for information, was quoted by the Jakarta Post newspaper as saying.
Party officials, beginning a three-day annual congress on Wednesday, said they hoped to increase Golkar's share of the vote to 71 percent in 1997.
Harmoko is expected to possibly announce a formal target at another news conference on Friday.
Golkar has said it will contest all 425 elective seats of the 500-member parliament in the elections scheduled for June next year. The other 75 seats are nominated by the military.

The other two political parties legally allowed to contest elections in Indonesia are the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP) and the Christian-Nationalist Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI).

In 1987 elections, Golkar won 73 percent of the vote. But in 1992, that share dropped to 68 percent of votes cast and 282 seats. The PPP won 17 percent and 62 seats, and the PDI 15 percent and 56 seats.
Only 400 seats were at stake in the previous elections, with the other 100 members being nominated.
The government-backed faction of the PDI submitted its lists of candidates for the 1997 poll last month.
However, supporters of former party leader Megawati Sukarnoputri, who was ousted at a congress in June, have lodged a suit with the state administrative court to challenge the validity of the list.
